subject: mathematics
title: Understand fractions and percentages
promise: This starts from the foundations and builds to the real-world questions — discounts, increases, and scores out of anything. The one idea underneath everything: a percentage is a fraction whose bottom number is 100.

sections.heading: A percentage is a fraction with 100 on the bottom
sections.body:
Per cent means out of every hundred, so every percentage is secretly a fraction: 35% is 35/100. That means you can turn ANY fraction into a percentage by finding its equivalent fraction with 100 on the bottom.
Take 7/20. Ask: what do I multiply 20 by to get 100? Five. So multiply top and bottom by 5: 7/20 = 35/100 = 35%.
This works whenever the bottom number divides into 100 — halves, quarters, fifths, tenths, twentieths, twenty-fifths and fiftieths all convert this way.
sections.example: 13/20 = 65/100 = 65%. And 9/25 = 36/100 = 36%, multiplying top and bottom by 4.

sections.heading: Going back: percentages as simplified fractions
sections.body:
The road runs both ways. 45% is 45/100 — but that fraction can be SIMPLIFIED by dividing top and bottom by the same number. 45 and 100 both divide by 5, so 45/100 = 9/20.
Simplifying does not change the amount, only the way it is written — like folding the same shirt more neatly.
The common ones are worth knowing on sight: 50% = 1/2, 25% = 1/4, 75% = 3/4, 20% = 1/5, 10% = 1/10, 5% = 1/20, 1% = 1/100.

sections.heading: Turning any score into a percentage
sections.body:
Real life rarely marks things out of 100. You score 12 out of 30 on a quiz — what percentage is that?
Write the score as a fraction first: 12/30. Simplify it: both divide by 6, so 12/30 = 2/5. Now convert to hundredths: 2/5 = 40/100 = 40%.
The pattern is always the same three moves: write it as a fraction, simplify if you can, then stretch it to hundredths. This is how test scores, survey results and match statistics all become percentages.

sections.heading: Two ways to find a percentage of an amount
sections.body:
Way one — the fraction method: swap the percentage for its fraction and take that fraction of the amount. 25% of 48? A quarter of 48 is 12.
Way two — the 10% building blocks: find 10% by dividing by 10, then assemble. 45% of 60? 10% is 6, so 40% is 24, and 5% is 3. Together: 24 + 3 = 27.
Neither way is more correct — pick whichever fits the numbers. Friendly fraction? Use way one. Awkward percentage like 35% or 65%? Blocks are usually quicker.
sections.example: 60% of 45: 10% is 4.5, so 60% is 4.5 × 6 = 27. Or: 60% = 3/5, and 3/5 of 45 is 27. Same answer, two roads.

sections.heading: More than the whole: percentages over 100
sections.body:
Nothing stops a percentage climbing past 100 — it just means MORE than the original whole. 100% of something is all of it, so 125% is all of it plus a quarter more.
As a decimal, 125% is 1.25, because 125 hundredths is one whole and 25 hundredths.
You meet this whenever something grows: a town's population becoming 150% of what it was means it is now one and a half times its old size. Over-100 percentages describe growth; under-100 percentages describe a part.
sections.example: 150% of 62: that is all of 62 plus half of 62 — 62 + 31 = 93.

sections.heading: Discounts and increases: the questions shops ask
sections.body:
A discount takes a percentage OFF. A jacket costs 40 and the sale says 20% off. First find the discount: 20% of 40 is 8. Then — and this is the step people skip — SUBTRACT it: 40 − 8 = 32. The price is 32, not 8.
An increase adds a percentage ON. A fare of 60 rises by 25%: the rise is 15, so the new fare is 60 + 15 = 75.
Always read the question twice: is it asking for the CHANGE (the 8, the 15) or the NEW AMOUNT (the 32, the 75)? Both answers appear in your working — the question decides which one to circle.
sections.example: 30% off a 50 book: the discount is 15, the new price is 35.

mistakes.wrong: Answering "8" when a 40 jacket has 20% off and the question asks the sale price.
mistakes.right: 8 is the DISCOUNT. The sale price is 40 − 8 = 32.
mistakes.why: Percentage-off questions have two numbers in them: the change and the new amount. Finish the subtraction before you answer.
You cannot just glue the digits together — 8 does not divide evenly into 100, so eighths give decimal percentages.

mistakes.wrong: Increasing 60 by 25% and getting 85 (adding the 25 itself).
mistakes.right: The increase is 25% OF 60, which is 15 — so the answer is 60 + 15 = 75.
mistakes.why: A percentage is never added directly. It must first be turned into an amount by taking it OF the number.

check.question: Which percentage is the same as 7/20?
Which percentage is the same as 3/8?
Write 125% as a decimal.
check.explanation: 125 hundredths is one whole and 25 hundredths: 1.25.

check.question: A 40 jacket is in a 20%-off sale. What is the sale price?
check.explanation: The discount is 20% of 40 = 8, and the price after taking it off is 40 − 8 = 32.

check.question: A player scores 12 out of 30. What percentage is that?
Which percentage is the same as 0.06?
Increase 60 by 25%. What is the new amount?
check.explanation: 25% of 60 is 15, and 60 + 15 = 75. The increase must be worked out as an amount first.

check.question: What is 4/5 of 35?
check.explanation: One fifth of 35 is 7, so four fifths is 7 × 4 = 28.

practice.hint: Tenths become hundredths when you multiply top and bottom by 10.
40% is four 10%-blocks, then add half a block.
Multiply top and bottom by 5 to reach hundredths.

practice.prompt: A player scores 24 out of 40. What percentage is that?
practice.hint: Simplify 24/40 first, then stretch to hundredths.
10% of 80 is 8: three blocks make 24, and 5% adds 4.

practice.prompt: Decrease 50 by 10%. What is the new amount?
practice.hint: Find 10% of 50 first, then take it away.
All of 62, plus half of 62 again.

practice.prompt: Increase 84 by 25%. What is the new amount?
practice.hint: A quarter of 84 is 21 — then add it on.
One eighth is 12.5%. How many eighths do you have?
